title: 7 weeks, 1,684 commits: Agents work night shifts on my game, I playtest and merge in the morning
author: Scared_Treacle_4894
selftext:
I'm building Limes: Rome Tower Defense. It's a 3D tower defense on the Roman frontier for iPhone, made in Godot 4.7 (Android is in progress). First commit: September 20. It's now in public TestFlight beta.

I designed the game, directed everything and played every mission. Claude Code wrote most of the code. Here's what that setup looks like after 7 weeks.

**Where it stands**

* Two campaigns: Germania (15 missions) and Britannia (12 missions). Floods, tides, burning bridges, fog of war, a convoy escort. A third campaign, Italia, is in progress.
* \~152k lines of GDScript, including tests. 326 registered test suites.
* 255 3D models, all generated by Blender Python scripts. No image-gen or 3D-gen assets.

**The workflow**

* **Plan first, always.** Every feature, bug or change gets a written plan in the repo. That's 566 plan folders so far. A reviewer agent critiques each plan before any code is written.
* **Separate implementer and reviewer.** The implementer works from the plan. An independent reviewer checks the result against the plan and a checklist. They loop until the review passes.
* **Models:** Sonnet 5.5 (medium) for code-heavy work, Opus 5.5 (medium) for graphics-heavy work, Opus 5.5 (low) as reviewer.
* **"Shifts."** I approve a batch of planned packages. Agents work through them one by one in git worktrees while I'm away. Afterwards I playtest and merge.
* **A written test plan.** It tells agents which suites a change needs. A full run takes about 90 minutes, so "run everything" isn't an option for every change.
* **Test-driven bug fixing.** Every fix must start with a failing test.

**Tools the agents built for themselves (I'd build them again)**

* **Bot playtester.** An autoplay bot plays each mission. It searches for the smallest budget it can still win with. A rough difficulty signal, sadly no substitute for humans.
* **Map review.** Renders a top-down view of every map: routes, build zones, tower ranges. Plus metrics like route length and coverage. Agents must run it before and after every map change.

![img](36lz279g5t0i1)

![img](cgs74sgk5t0i1)

* **Visual loop.** For art changes, one agent implements, another scores screenshots against a reference image. Round by round, until a threshold is reached.
* **Device measurements.** Load tests run on a real iPhone. A ledger tracks every performance change, before and after. Right now I'm moving hot paths to native C++ (GDExtension), starting with terrain.

**What didn't work (or still doesn't)**

* **Docs rot fast.** At this pace, README and design docs contradict each other within days. Agents now have a rule: trust code and tests over old docs.
* **Bots aren't players.** The bot beats every mission. But the balance has had almost no human input. That's why there's a beta (link in the comments).
* **Parallel sessions collide.** Several agents in one checkout kept switching branches under each other. Worktrees fixed most of it, plus a rule to check the current branch before merging.
* **Agents happily optimize the wrong thing.** One plan built a slimmed-down Godot export template to speed up startup. On the iPhone, startup time didn't change. The app got only \~5% smaller, so we dropped it. New rule: measure on the device before believing anything.

**Questions for you**

* How do you balance difficulty when your only tester is a bot?
* How do you keep docs in sync with agent-written code? Or do you let them go?

If you want to try it, the iPhone beta link is in the comments. Happy to go into detail on any part of the setup.

comments.author: -FlyingPenguin-
comments.body:
Sent you an email!

\- I dont think bots can determine whats “fun”. This is a bottleneck you and testers will have to determine. You will also have to use people that are not you, because you are probably very good at your own game.

\- Personally, I dont think anything other than a high level overview is needed for docs, unless you are working in a team, or have a complex system. When I add onto a system, I will say something like “Add drifting. It should feel like X,Y,Z”. If im building a new system, and it is large, I will typically make a plan first, with claude inside the project. This should be enough (on latest claude models) to account for your architecture, in my experience. 

Complex systems like multiplayer may need more than just a plan, and definitely need docs. You dont want to prompt an llm to know basic details around your matchmaking logic.

replies.author: Scared_Treacle_4894
replies.body:

replies.author: Scared_Treacle_4894
replies.body:
Most visuals come out of a structured loop rather than hand-tuning. Here’s this camp rampart:

https://i.redd.it/wlreeujskx0i1.png

1. Rough first pass: I start with an initial implementation and only a vague direction (“earth rampart with a ditch”). Gameplay works, but it looks generic (far left).

2. Target image: I generate a reference image with ChatGPT from a screenshot plus a description of what I want. It’s a target, not a spec.

3. Image loop: Then AI agents (Claude Code) iterate in rounds:

* One agent implements changes.
* A script renders the same fixed camera shots every round.
* A *separate* reviewer agent scores them against the reference on a fixed rubric: wall shape, grass, exposed earth, ditch, blending, overall look.
* The next round targets the lowest scores, and every round is a commit.

Scores: 27 → 53 → 60 → 64 → 64 → 64. Round 1 brought the big jump: the ditch is now actually cut into the terrain. After five rounds progress stalled below the target of 80, so I picked the last round.

The key: a fixed camera, a fixed rubric and a reviewer who never sees the implementer’s reasoning keep the iteration honest.

replies.author: FondantIcy866
replies.body: Awesome ty! So in step 3, by script you mean, claude is generating the image w code, and/or in blender?

replies.author: Scared_Treacle_4894
replies.body:
The “script” doesn’t generate images: It just starts the real game, puts the camera in the same spots every round and takes screenshots. The models itself (eg. the ditch or people) are built by Python scripts that Claude writes and runs in Blender, so I don’t model anything by hand. 

The people are made the same way, from simple body parts. Their animations are calculated in code instead of being animated by hand: when walking (for example) each foot stays on the ground until it steps forward.
